turns.doctor_question: Hello. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, doctor, I... I suppose I'm here because the folks at my church are getting worried about me, and, well, to be honest, I'm getting a bit worried too. I've been helping out in the fellowship hall for years and years, you know, setting up for the meals and making sure everything is nice. I never finished much school, so I always took pride in being a hard worker with my hands. But lately, I just keep doing these... these odd things, and I don't even realize I'm doing them right away. 

Like, we have our potluck, and I'll be working the food line. But the other Sunday, I was standing right there by the potluck table, and I had the big serving spoon for the casserole, and I just... I just held it up in the air. I lifted it up to serve, and I just stood there, not moving at all. Just completely frozen with my arm up in the air. I don't even know how long I was standing like that, just staring, until somebody had to gently take the spoon right out of my hand. 

And then another time, just recently, I was in charge of the paper goods. I was folding the napkins, the little cheap paper ones we get from the dollar store. But I got stuck. I was just folding the exact same stack of napkins over and over and over again. Just smoothing them down and creasing them, the very same ones, while all those nice people were just standing in a long line waiting on me to finish so they could get their supper. I don't know why I get stuck doing things like that, but it's just so embarrassing to be holding up the whole church line, and I just can't seem to help it.

turns.patient_response:
Well, that's the strange part, doctor. It's like... it's like nothing at all. Or maybe everything at once? I don't rightly know how to explain it. When I was holding that big metal spoon—it was one of those heavy serving spoons, the kind with the little slots in it for the green bean casserole, because you don't want all that extra juice getting on the paper plates and making them soggy before folks even sit down—well, my mind just went sort of... blank. 

It wasn't like I was daydreaming about what I needed to get at the grocery store, or worrying about my sister's hip surgery, or anything normal like that. It was just an empty space in my head. I remember looking at the shiny part of the spoon, and the way the lights in the fellowship hall—they have those long fluorescent tubes in the ceiling that always hum just a little bit if you listen close—how the light was reflecting off it. And that was it. Just the spoon and the light. 

And with the napkins, those little square ones, they were the pale yellow ones that day because Pastor Thomas likes the cheerful colors for the spring potlucks... I just felt like I had to make the crease perfectly flat. My mind wasn't telling me a story or thinking about the people waiting. It was just stuck on the edge of that napkin, over and over. Smoothing it down. It's so embarrassing when I come back to myself and realize what I've been doing, because I'm usually so sharp about keeping the line moving. I've always prided myself on that, you know? Making sure everyone gets their plate filled up nice and quick. But in those moments, it's just... quiet. Just a big, empty quiet in my head.
